answers.headline: No. Since July 2015 it’s banned to drive with earphones, an earpiece or a headset in your ear.
answers.summary: The ban covers any sound device worn in or on the ear, including for phone calls, music or navigation. It applies to drivers of cars and motorcycles; motorcyclists may only use devices built into the helmet.
answers.penalties: A fine and points taken off your licence.

answers.headline: No. The limit is 0.5 g/l of blood, or 0.2 g/l for new and learner drivers.
answers.summary: It’s banned to drive with 0.5 g/l of alcohol in the blood or more (0.25 mg/l in breath). Drivers with a probationary licence and learners in accompanied driving have a limit of 0.2 g/l (0.10 mg/l in breath). From 0.8 g/l, or when visibly drunk, it’s a criminal offence (délit).
conditions: General limit: 0.5 g/l blood (0.25 mg/l breath)
Probationary licence and accompanied driving: 0.2 g/l (0.10 mg/l breath)
answers.penalties: Below 0.8 g/l: up to €750 (usually a €135 fixed fine), 6 points and possible suspension. 0.8 g/l or more: up to 3 years in prison and a €9,000 fine. Refusing a test: the same as 0.8 g/l or more.

answers.headline: Yes. In France no law requires you to have an ID card, let alone carry one.
answers.summary: No law obliges you to own or carry an identity card. If police check your identity, you can prove it by other means, such as a birth certificate, voter card or student card, but the check takes longer and you can be held for up to 4 hours while your identity is established.
conditions: You may have to prove your identity some other way during a check

answers.headline: No. Using or possessing cannabis is a crime in France, usually punished with an on-the-spot €500 fine.
answers.summary: Using drugs, including cannabis, is a délit. If you’re caught using or with a small amount, police can issue a fixed fine without a trial. Larger amounts, hard drugs or a criminal record lead to court instead.
answers.penalties: Fixed fine: €500 (€400 if paid within 15 days, €1,000 if unpaid after 45 days). In court: up to 1 year in prison and a €3,750 fine.

answers.headline: No. Theft is a crime in France, with up to 3 years in prison and a €45,000 fine.
answers.summary: Simple theft (vol simple) is a délit. The penalty is the same if you give the item back afterwards or only attempted the theft. Theft with aggravating circumstances, such as violence or breaking in, is punished more heavily.
answers.penalties: Simple theft: up to 3 years in prison and a €45,000 fine; more with aggravating circumstances.

answers.headline: Only through the car’s own system or speakers. Holding the phone, or using an earpiece, is banned.
answers.summary: Holding a phone while driving is banned, and so is wearing earphones, an earpiece or a headset. Using the car’s built-in hands-free system or loudspeaker isn’t covered by these bans, but you must still drive safely.
answers.penalties: Holding a phone: €135 fixed fine and 3 points. A prefect can also suspend your licence for up to 6 months without waiting for a court.
